To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we found that perceivers from two different countries (UK and China) and two different ethnic groups (Caucasian and Asian) agreed on three dimensions of facial impressions, and the models of these dimensions explained 75% of the variability of impressions.
we found strong evidence for a common approachability dimension and some evidence of a capability dimension, but not dominance.
the three dimensions of facial impressions are universal, and that they are based on adaptive cues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how people form first impressions of faces.
the nature of facial impressions across culture and their underlying psychological mechanisms, which may have evolved to detect threat and/or sexual partners.
the question of whether there is a universal set of cues to social evaluation that are based on evolved adaptations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the facial impressions of British and Chinese perceivers of Asian and Caucasian male faces were very similar, but that British perceivers were less sensitive than Chinese perceivers to the effects of facial hair on attractiveness and dominance.
the three dimensions of facial first impressions are universal, but the relative weightings of these dimensions are not.
there is a high degree of universality in the dimensions of facial impression across cultures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
facial appearance is a universal cue to social impressions.
we have found evidence for common facial impression dimensions across culture.
we found evidence for a universal set of dimensions underlying first impressions of faces.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people across culture share the same basic facial impressions.
, while some aspects of the facial impression process may differ across cultures, there are many similarities that are likely to be based on common adaptive functions.
, despite the fact that facial impressions can have important consequences, they may not be as culturally specific or arbitrary as one might think.
